passage: On a wet Sunday, ten-year-old Pranav opened a building set with four hundred pieces and a picture of a crane on the box. His mother Rekha called him for lunch. He did not hear. She called again, and he waved a hand. When she came in, the plate was cold, the light had changed, and he was fitting the last arm in place, tongue between his teeth. "Was it hard?" she asked. "Just hard enough," he said, and blinked as if waking up. Five years later, Pranav sat cross-legged with a guitar, working a chord change that kept buzzing. His friend Kunal texted about a game night, and the phone buzzed on the bed. Pranav did not touch it. He played the change slowly, then a bit faster, until his fingers landed clean. When he looked up, an hour had gone. His shoulders were loose and his mind felt clear. He picked up the phone at last, typed to Kunal that he'd come after dinner, and went back to the strings for one more round.

qa.q: What was pictured on the box of Pranav's building set?
qa.a: The box had a picture of a crane on it.

qa.q: How is Pranav's absorption at ten similar to and different from his practice at fifteen?
qa.a: At ten he lost track of lunch and light while building the crane, and at fifteen he lost track of time and his phone while working the chord change. Both tasks were hard enough to need his attention, and both left him calm and clear.

qa.q: What was Pranav probably feeling when he said the crane was just hard enough?
qa.a: He felt quietly satisfied and pleasantly challenged, and he seemed to wake up from being absorbed.

qa.q: What could Pranav do to keep enjoying this kind of focus?
qa.a: He could pick pieces or songs a little harder than the last, and keep his phone away while he works on them. 🙂

grounding: The same person shows flow at two ages: absorbed in a building set as a child and in guitar practice as a teenager, when the task suits his skill.
